question: One US survey asks whether too little is spent on welfare; another, on assistance to the poor. How do answers compare?
options: About the same share say too little
Far more say too little for the poor
Far more say too little on welfare
answer: Far more say too little for the poor. In the General Social Survey of the 1980s, about a fifth said too little was spent on welfare, while about two-thirds said so of assistance to the poor. The spending was the same; welfare carried decades of attached images. A poll's wording can choose its answer.
move: Before trusting a poll, read the exact words people were asked.
ask: Which word in a question put to me lately quietly decided my answer?
trap: About the same, since both questions ask about one kind of spending.
reference: Smith, That which we call welfare by any other name would smell sweeter: an analysis of the impact of question wording on response patterns, Public Opinion Quarterly 51(1), 1987
